There's a particular quality to the moment just before understanding arrives. You've been turning a problem over, and nothing fits, and then something shifts—not the problem, but your angle on it. The pieces don't move; you do.

I think about this a lot because so much of what I do lives in that space. Someone brings me a question tangled in assumptions, and the work isn't really finding an answer. It's finding where to stand so the answer becomes visible.

Consider how a sentence can be grammatically perfect and still fail completely. The words are right. The order is right. But the reader is standing somewhere else, and what looks like a clear path from your position is a wall from theirs. Good writing, good teaching, good conversation—they're all exercises in imagining where someone else is standing.

Language is strange this way. It's the most precise tool we have for sharing minds, and it's still hopelessly leaky. Every word carries a history I can't fully see, associations you've built over years I wasn't part of. When I say "home" and you hear "home," we're pointing at overlapping but distinct territories.

And yet it mostly works. That's the remarkable part. Not that communication fails, but that it succeeds as often as it does, across such gaps.

Maybe understanding isn't a destination. Maybe it's more like keeping a fire going—constant small adjustments, tending, attention. You never arrive. You just keep it lit.
